configuration options. ::properties ::property name: 'apikey', type: 'string' your api authentication key. required for all requests. ::property name: 'timeout', type: 'integer' request timeout in milliseconds. defaults to 30000. ::property name: 'retries', type: 'integer' number of retry attempts for failed requests. defaults to 3. ::property name: 'debug', type: 'boolean' enable debug logging for troubleshooting. defaults to false. :: usage: --- layout columns id: 'layout-columns' create multi-column layouts for side-by-side content. ::row ::col left column this content appears in the left title: Authentication
description: In this guide, we'll look at how authentication works. Protocol offers two ways to authenticate your API requests: Basic authentication and OAuth2 with a token.
content: authentication you'll need to authenticate your requests to access any of the endpoints in the protocol api. in this guide, we'll look at how authentication works. protocol offers two ways to authenticate your api requests: basic authentication and oauth2 with a token — oauth2 is the recommended way. classname: 'lead' basic authentication with basic authentication, you use your username and password to authenticate your http requests. unless you have a very good reason, you probably shouldn't use basic auth. here's how to authenticate using curl: please don't commit your protocol password to github! oauth2 with bearer token the recommended way to authenticate with the protocol api is by using oauth2. when establishing a connection using oauth2, you will need your access token — you will find it in the protocol dashboard under api settings. here's how to add the token to the request header using curl: always keep your token safe and reset it if you suspect it has been compromised. using an sdk if you use one of our official sdks, you won't have to worry about any of the above — fetch your access token from the protocol dashboard under api settings, and the client library will take care of the rest. all the client libraries use oauth2 behind the scenes. ::button url: '/sdks', variant: 'text' check out our list of first-party sdks ::icon arrow-right ::

title: Pagination
description: In this guide, we will look at how to work with paginated responses when querying the Protocol API
content: pagination in this guide, we will look at how to work with paginated responses when querying the protocol api. by default, all responses limit results to ten. however, you can go as high as 100 by adding a parameter to your requests. if you are using one of the official protocol api client libraries, you don't need to worry about pagination, as it's all being taken care of behind the scenes. classname: 'lead' when an api response returns a list of objects, no matter the amount, pagination is supported. in paginated responses, objects are nested in a attribute and have a attribute that indicates whether you have reached the end of the last page. you can use the and query parameters to browse pages. example using cursors ::row ::col in this example, we request the page that starts after the conversation with id . as a result, we get a list of three conversations and can tell by the attribute that we have reached the end of the resultset. ::properties ::property name: 'startingafter', type: 'string' the last id on the page you're currently on when you want to fetch the next page. ::property name: 'endingbefore', type: 'string' the first id on the page you're currently on when you want to fetch the previous page. ::property name: 'limit', type: 'integer' limit the number of items returned. :: ::col ::

title: Errors
description: In this guide, we will talk about what happens when something goes wrong while you work with the API.
content: errors in this guide, we will talk about what happens when something goes wrong while you work with the api. mistakes happen, and mostly they will be yours, not ours. let's look at some status codes and error types you might encounter. classname: 'lead' you can tell if your request was successful by checking the status code when receiving an api response. if a response comes back unsuccessful, you can use the error type and error message to figure out what has gone wrong and do some rudimentary debugging before contacting support. ::callout before reaching out to support with an error, please be aware that 99% of all reported errors are, in fact, user errors. therefore, please carefully check your code before contacting protocol support. :: error types ::row ::col whenever a request is unsuccessful, the protocol api will return an error response with an error type and message. you can use this information to understand better what has gone wrong and how to fix it. most of the error messages are pretty helpful and actionable. here is a list of the two error types supported by the protocol api — use these to understand what you have done wrong. ::properties ::property name: 'apierror' this means that we made an error, which is highly speculative and unlikely. ::property name: 'invalidrequest' this means that you made an error, which is much more likely. :: ::col ::

title: Installation Guide
description: Complete step-by-step guide for installing NoMercy.
content: installation requirements before installing nomercy, ensure your system meets the following requirements: - operating system: windows 10+, macos 10.12+, or linux ubuntu 20.04+ recommended - memory: minimum 4gb ram 8gb recommended - storage: at least 10gb free space for application and database - network: stable internet connection for initial setup installation steps 1. download nomercy visit the official nomercy github repository and download the latest release suitable for your operating system. 2. extract files extract the downloaded archive to your preferred installation directory: 3. run installation script execute the installation script appropriate for your system: 4. configure basic settings during installation, you'll be prompted to: - set the installation directory - configure database connection - set up initial admin account - configure media storage paths 5. start the service after installation, start the nomercy service: verification to verify successful installation, access the nomercy web interface: - url: http://localhost:7000 default - admin account: use the credentials you created during installation next steps once installed: 1. configure mediaserver - set up media storage 2. add content - start adding your entertainment files 3. access the web interface to begin organizing your library troubleshooting if you encounter installation issues: - check that your system meets the minimum requirements - ensure all required ports are available default: 7000, 7001 - review the installation logs in the directory - consult the faq or open an issue on github getting help for additional support: - visit the nomercy documentation - check out the mediaserver guide - open an issue on the github repository

title: MediaServer Overview
description: Comprehensive overview of NoMercy MediaServer component.
content: what is mediaserver? mediaserver is a core component of nomercy that handles media file storage, organization, and streaming. it provides efficient management of your entertainment content library with powerful indexing and search capabilities. key features media organization - automatic cataloging: automatically detect and categorize media files - smart tagging: intelligent tagging system for content discovery - folder structure: flexible organization supporting complex folder hierarchies - multi-format support: support for various video, audio, and image formats streaming capabilities - direct streaming: stream media directly to supported devices - format transcoding: automatic transcoding for optimal playback quality - adaptive bitrate: intelligent bitrate adjustment for different connection speeds - subtitle support: automatic subtitle detection and management performance & reliability - efficient indexing: fast indexing for quick content discovery - caching system: intelligent caching for improved performance - backup support: built-in backup and recovery mechanisms - monitoring: real-time monitoring of media library health supported media formats video formats - mp4, mkv, avi, mov, flv, webm, and more audio formats - mp3, flac, aac, ogg, wav, and more image formats - jpg, png, webp, gif, and more components mediaserver consists of several components: 1. indexer: scans and catalogs media files 2. database: stores metadata and configuration 3. streamer: handles media playback and delivery 4. monitor: tracks system health and performance getting started with mediaserver to get started with mediaserver: 1. configure mediaserver - set up paths and settings 2. add media folders to your library 3. let the indexer scan and organize your content 4. start streaming and enjoying your media next steps - configuration guide - detailed setup instructions - nomercy getting started - return to main guide - installation guide - complete installation reference

title: MediaServer Configuration
description: How to configure NoMercy MediaServer using startup flags, environment variables, and the in-app web UI.
content: there is no config file nomercy mediaserver has no configuration file. there is no , , , or file to edit. settings are controlled in two places: - startup flags or environment variables — port, ip address, log level, and a few launch-time options - web ui — everything else: libraries, users, encoder settings, and general preferences open after the server starts to reach the dashboard. environment variables every flag has a matching environment variable. environment variables are applied when the corresponding flag is not passed. this is the primary way to configure docker deployments. | variable | equivalent flag | example | |:--|:--|:--| | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | --- docker: the hostip requirement when running in docker, the container cannot auto-detect your host machine's lan ip. you must supply it via the environment variable, which the provided compose files map from a shell variable. the compose file contains: if you skip this step, the server starts but clients on other devices may not be able to discover or connect to it. you can also hard-code the value directly in the compose file instead of using the shell variable. for gpu-accelerated transcoding, use the matching compose variant: --- adding libraries via the web ui after first login, add your media libraries through the web dashboard. navigate to settings > libraries, then click add library. choose the library type movies, tv shows, or music, give it a name, and select the folder path where your media files live. the server will begin scanning immediately. library paths must be accessible to the server process. for docker, this means the folder must be mounted as a volume in your compose file. the provided compose template includes commented-out volume entries under , , and — uncomment and adjust those paths to match your actual media locations before starting the container. --- port forwarding to access your server from outside your home network, forward port or whichever port you configured on your router to your server's lan ip. once a certificate is issued during first-run setup, the server uses https automatically. --- next steps - title: What is the Music Player
description: The NoMercy Music Player — headless, plugin-driven, event-driven. Architecture overview and relation to the player kit.
content: what is the nomercy music player is a headless, typescript-first audio player for browsers. it handles playback, queue management, crossfade, lyric sync, and eq — with no ui in the core package. every visual element is either a plugin or built by the consumer. layer diagram --- key design decisions no ui in core. renders nothing. the is optional and produces a configurable dom overlay. consumers who want full control render their own ui from player events. generic playlist item. — defaults to but consumers extend it with their own fields without wrapping or adapting. plugin-everything. lyrics, media session, cast, eq, key handling — all plugins. register only what you need. plugins are removed from the bundle via tree-shaking when not imported. backend swappable at runtime. switch between and with . custom backends inject via . --- what it is not - not a ui framework component no vue/react component — see framework integration - not a video player no subtitle tracks, no quality levels — see nomercy-video-player - not server-side — runs in the browser only --- see also - installation — install and import paths - quick start — minimal working player - player kit — shared infrastructure documentation

title: Installation
description: Install nomercy-music-player via npm, yarn, or pnpm. Requirements and import paths.
content: installation requirements - node.js 18 or later tooling only — the player itself runs in any modern browser - a module bundler vite, webpack, rollup, or similar import paths the package ships two import paths: importing plugins from the main entry point is not supported — always use . --- typescript the package ships full typescript declarations. no package is needed. the recommended type for a consumer-held player reference is : use the concrete type only when you need access to internals not exposed on the interface. --- browser support | browser | minimum version | notes | | --------------- | --------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | | chrome | 90 | full support | | firefox | 90 | full support | | safari | 15 | web audio crossfade supported; native hls skips | | edge | 90 | full support | | ios safari | 15.4 | web audio may require user gesture before | | android webview | 90 | audio output routing not available | --- hls streams hls support is handled by , which is a regular production dependency of the package. no separate install is needed. the library is loaded automatically when an url is detected on a browser that does not support native hls. on safari and ios, native hls is used directly and is not loaded. --- what to read next - quick start — minimal working player in under 30 lines - configuration — all options

title: AutoAdvancePlugin
description: Autonomous queue advance with optional preload, crossfade, and custom ended/preload/crossfade handlers.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-music-player-v2/src/plugins/auto-advance/index.ts / autoadvanceplugin most players need nothing more than "when the current track ends, play the next one." that is exactly what does by default. you can also tell it to buffer the next track a few seconds early, or hand off to a crossfade instead of a hard cut. the plugin wires to two player events: for the actual advance, and for the early-warning preload and crossfade path. the one time you leave this plugin out is when something else already drives , such as a websocket sync layer or a cast session orchestrator. in that case let the orchestrator call and skip this plugin entirely. plugin id: options | option | type | default | description | | ------ | ---- | ------- | ----------- | | | | | master toggle. set to to pause all auto-advance behaviour without removing the plugin. | | | | | when , calls on the event, buffering the next track before it is needed. | | | | | when , calls on the event. | | | | | crossfade duration in seconds when . means a hard cut. set this to match or be less than in the player config. | methods force-advance to the next track immediately, regardless of playback state. calls . peek the queue head and load it into the next slot. no-ops when there is no next track. safe to call at any time. register an additional callback that runs after the built-in advance logic. use this for analytics, logging, or server sync that should follow the queue advance. register an additional handler for preload behaviour. is the upcoming track, or when the queue is exhausted. register an additional handler for crossfade behaviour. is the resolved in seconds. execution order when fires: 1. if , calls 2. if and there is a next track, calls 3. all registered run 4. all registered run when fires: 1. calls 2. all registered run registration with options: full example with crossfade, preload, and an analytics hook: see also - title: CastSenderPlugin
description: Music Chromecast sender, a thin specialisation of the kit base that maps music fields to MusicTrackMediaMetadata and sets audio/mpeg as the default content type.

want your music player to cast to a chromecast device. it opens the cast session picker, forwards the current track to the receiver, and keeps the receiver in sync as the user plays, pauses, seeks, and changes tracks. when the receiver disconnects, the plugin restores local playback from the receiver's last position. the music-specific work this class does is small: it sets as the default content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-kit/src/plugins/tab-leader/index.ts re-exported verbatim by packages/nomercy-music-player-v2/src/plugins/tab-leader/index.ts / tableaderplugin if your app can be open in multiple tabs at the same time, you have probably seen two tabs fighting over audio. stops that by using the web locks api to elect one tab as the leader. only the leader tab is allowed to play. when a second tab acquires the lock, the first tab loses the lock; title: Backends Overview
description: Choosing between AudioElementBackend and WebAudioBackend — capabilities, crossfade accuracy, and platform constraints.

title: AudioElementBackend
description: HTML5 audio element backend with lazy Web Audio graph and RAF-based crossfade — the default music player backend.
content: audioelementbackend the default audio backend. uses a native element for transport and optionally creates a when a plugin requests the web audio graph. kind: hls support when the audio url ends with and the browser does not support native hls: 1. the backend imports a regular production dependency 2. creates an instance and calls + 3. all subsequent segment fetches are handled by on safari and ios, native hls is used directly and is skipped. --- web audio graph lazy the backend creates only when the first plugin calls or . until then, the element routes directly to the system output. this means and work with this backend — at a slight cost: once the is created, it cannot be removed for the lifetime of the backend instance. --- crossfade implementation crossfade is driven by a loop at ~50 fps. a secondary element is allocated via , pre-rolled via , and then both elements are gain-ramped in opposite directions over . - primary ramps from current volume to 0 - secondary ramps from 0 to current volume - at completion, the secondary becomes the primary element and the old primary is discarded accuracy: ±20 ms one raf frame. use for sub-millisecond accuracy. --- secondary gain api returns when no secondary element is allocated. --- output routing is available in chrome and chromium-based browsers. safari does not support it. --- see also - backends overview — when to choose vs - iaudiobackend — full interface reference - webaudiobackend — sample-accurate alternative

title: WebAudioBackend
description: Web Audio API pipeline backend with sample-accurate crossfade via linearRampToValueAtTime.
content: webaudiobackend web audio pipeline backend. routes all audio through a graph. crossfade uses for sample-accurate ramps. kind: audio graph the backend constructs a graph rooted at the : when is registered, it connects its effect chain between the and . --- hls fallback hls streams always use because requires a element. pure file playback mp3, aac, flac, ogg uses for sample-accurate decoding. --- crossfade implementation : 1. primary ramps from current volume to 0 via 2. secondary ramps from 0 to current volume via 3. both ramps complete at 4. at completion, the secondary becomes the primary; the old primary is disconnected and its buffer released accuracy: sample-accurate. no raf loop, no jitter. volume changes are smoothed with a 10 ms ramp to prevent clicks on mute/unmute or abrupt volume changes. --- ios considerations on ios and in some mobile chrome contexts, creation may be suspended until a user gesture. if , call inside a user interaction handler before starting playback. --- graph access --- see also - backends overview — when to choose vs - iaudiobackend — full interface reference - audioelementbackend — default, less accurate alternative - advanced: equalizer customization — building on the web audio graph

title: Troubleshooting
description: Common music player issues — no audio, crossfade not firing, lyrics out of sync, backend errors, and diagnostics.
content: troubleshooting does nothing symptom: call appears to succeed but no audible transition occurs. causes and fixes: 1. selected — the default backend uses a loop for crossfade ~50 fps. it is less accurate than . crossfade is functional but may be imperceptible on short durations. switch with for sample-accurate fades. 2. duration too short — the default is 5 seconds. if your track is shorter than the fade duration, the crossfade completes instantly. reduce in . 3. already transitioning — returns . wait for the event before starting another. 4. fired first — if track end and your manual call overlap, the plugin may have already advanced. use and in options instead of calling manually from . --- lyrics are not displayed symptom: is registered but no lyrics appear. causes and fixes: 1. no on the track — calls which falls back to . if neither is set, no fetch occurs. check your . 2. not registered — if you have not called , the plugin uses directly. this still works if the url is correct. 3. unsupported file extension — parser selection is by url extension. and are built-in. custom formats need . 4. cors blocked — the fetch must succeed from the browser. add headers on the lyric host or proxy through your own server. 5. event not fired — listen to . if it never fires, check the network tab for a failed fetch on the lyrics url. --- lyrics are out of sync symptom: lyrics display at the wrong time. causes and fixes: 1. lrc timestamp format — verify your file uses format. non-standard formats e.g. seconds-only will not parse correctly. 2. seek position not updating lyrics — if the user seeks, re-scans from the cue list. this is automatic. if it is not working, ensure you are listening to not polling . 3. clock drift with — the uses which is sample-accurate but may diverge from after long sessions. this is expected. use not for any sync you build. --- throws symptom: throws an error. causes and fixes: 1. safari and ios — requires a user gesture on ios. call only inside a click or touch handler. 2. context suspended — the may be suspended after a page visibility change. listen to and call on page show. 3. already using the requested backend — not an error, but verify with before switching. --- --- phase stuck in symptom: returns indefinitely. causes and fixes: 1. source url returns a non-media content-type — hls streams must return . mp3/flac must return an audio content-type. a redirect to a login page returns , which hangs the parser. 2. auth token expired and is not set — a 401 with no refresh config produces a stale request. provide in your setup config. 3. hls manifest parse error — enable debug logging to capture the raw error. --- debug logging enable verbose output: with , the player logs every event, state title: FAQ
description: Frequently asked questions about the NoMercy Music Player — setup, crossfade, lyrics, backends, and TypeScript.
content: faq what is the difference between and ? is the concrete class. is the interface you should use for consumer-held references props, context, dependency injection. this prevents consumers from depending on the concrete constructor and keeps the type boundary clean. --- how many player instances can i have? as many as you need. each call with a unique id creates an independent instance. they share no state and each has its own audio backend, queue, and plugin set. a typical app has one global instance. a multi-room app might have one per room. --- does the player work server-side ssr/node? no. the player requires browser apis: , , , . it will throw on import in a node environment. in ssr frameworks next.js, nuxt, import and initialize only in browser-side code. --- why does autoplay block in the browser? browsers require a user gesture before allowing audio playback. common patterns: - call inside a or event handler. - on page load, set up the player and queue, but defer until the first interaction. the event fires when setup is complete. you can queue tracks there, but do not call from unless you know a user gesture has already occurred. --- what formats are supported? | format | notes | | ------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | | mp3 | universal | | aac / m4a | universal | | flac | all modern browsers | | ogg / opus | chrome, firefox, edge not safari | | wav | universal | | hls | native on safari; handles other browsers | the player ships as a production dependency. no extra install required for hls. --- how do i crossfade? two ways: 1. automatic — use with and . the plugin starts the crossfade automatically before each track ends. 2. manual — call from your own code. the default backend uses a loop ~50 fps. for sample-accurate fades, switch to first: --- what is the difference between and backends? | | | | | --------------------- | ------------------------------- | ---------------------- | | default | yes | no | | crossfade accuracy | ~50 fps raf | sample-accurate | | eq / spectrum plugins | via lazy mediaelementsourcenode | native web audio graph | | ios autoplay | easier | requires user gesture | | memory overhead | lower | slightly higher | switch at any time with . --- can i switch backends at runtime? yes. disposes the current backend, creates the new one, and re-wires all events. playback pauses during the switch. resume with . --- how do i persist volume / shuffle / repeat preferences? implement a and pass it in setup: the kit automatically reads and writes , , , and through the storage adapter. --- how do i add lyrics? 1. add to the player. 2. set on each must be a or url. 3. listen to for the active line. see lyrics for full details. --- can i use a custom lyric format? yes. register a : parser selection is by url extension. the built-in lrc and vtt parsers are registered by default. --- how do i show a spectrum analyzer or equalizer? both require which routes audio through a web audio graph and . and are re-exported from the music player's subpath for ergonomic imports: --- how do i integrate with react? use a custom hook with for the player instance and for reactive state. see react integration for the complete pattern. --- how do i integrate with vue? use a composable with for reactive state. see vue integration for the complete pattern. --- is typescript required? no, but strongly recommended. all events, methods, and configuration options are typed. without typescript you lose autocomplete and will have to consult the docs for every method signature. --- how do i clean up the player? call . this stops playback, removes all event listeners, disposes all plugins, frees the audio backend, and removes the instance from the internal registry. after , calling creates a fresh instance. --- see also - troubleshooting — error diagnosis - quick start — minimal working example - configuration — all setup options

title: Architecture
description: The five-layer model that separates generic player infrastructure from your application code. How kit, libraries, and plugins relate to each other.
content: architecture the player sdk is built on a strict five-layer model. every piece of code has a designated layer, and no layer may reach "down" into a layer below it or "up" into a layer above it without going through a defined port. why this matters the boundary between layer 4 and layer 5 is the enforcement point. anything nomercy-specific lives at layer 5. built-in plugins layer 4 must work for any consumer, with any backend, without any knowledge of the nomercy infrastructure. the practical consequence: when you add a built-in plugin from the package, it does not import from your app. when you write a consumer plugin, it can import from anywhere, but it should not modify kit internals. --- adapter ports layer 2 kit exposes a set of named adapter ports. each port has a typed interface and a default implementation. you replace a port only when you need different behavior, for example swapping for , or replacing the browser network monitor with a capacitor native adapter. the video and music library layers add ports of their own on top of these, documented with each library. see kit — adapters for the full port catalog. --- plugin layering in practice a typical app setup: layer-5 plugins can listen to events from layer-4 plugins using the typed class-form: --- three-package layout | npm package | layer | consumers | | -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | | 2 kit + 4 built-in plugins | library authors, advanced consumers writing plugins directly against the kit | | | 3 + 4 | anyone building a video player | | | 3 + 4 | anyone building a music player | both library packages re-export everything from the kit, so consumers of the video or music player do not need to install the kit separately unless they are writing kit-level plugins. --- container class system boundary state classes on the player container element are applied by the kit's container-class-emit mixin — , , , , etc. these are kit-level, present regardless of which ui plugin is active. the ui overlay controls bar, seek bar, menus, spinner is 's domain. it reads the kit's state classes and adds its own dom into the container. never modifies state classes — it only reads them. this boundary is intentional: a consumer can build a completely custom ui plugin that responds to the same state classes without touching . the state source kit and the ui renderer plugin are decoupled. the exact class inventory and which mixin owns each class is tracked by the player-architect spine. pending spine's confirmation, assume: , , , , , , , are kit-owned. , , are -owned.

title: Plugins and Adapters
description: The two ways to extend the player, the boundary between them, and when to reach for each.
content: plugins and adapters the player core is small on purpose. it plays a queue, keeps time, and fires events, and that's about it. everything else you build on top of it happens through one of two mechanisms, and almost every "how do i add x" question really comes down to picking the right one of the two. adapters swap how something already works an adapter replaces a piece of behavior the player already has with your own version. we call each swappable piece a port. the player always saves settings somewhere, always talks to the network somehow, always reads a clock. each of those is a port with a sensible default already in it. you swap the default when it doesn't fit you, like saving state to your own server instead of the browser. everything else keeps working, because the player only ever talks to the port, never to your implementation directly. if you catch yourself wanting an existing job done differently, you want an adapter. see adapters for all 28 ports and how to wire them. --- when to use which one question sorts almost every case: are you adding something new, or changing something that's already there? - adding something the player didn't do before, that's a plugin. - changing how an existing job gets done, that's an adapter. an equalizer is new behavior, so it's a plugin. saving to your server instead of the browser is the same job done differently, so it's an adapter. and the two team up all the time: a plugin can read from a storage port you swapped, where the plugin brings the behavior and the adapter decides where the data actually lives. for how all of this maps onto the player's layers, from the generic core up to your own app code, read architecture.

title: Auth & Fetch
description: The authFetch wrapper, bearer token injection, 401 vs 403 handling, and retry policy.
content: auth & fetch the player's pipeline handles all network requests made by the player and its built-in plugins. bearer tokens are injected automatically, 401 responses trigger a single refresh attempt, and 403 responses propagate immediately. configuration all fields are optional. without , requests are unauthenticated. --- auth config reference token or factory. a factory is called on every authenticated request — use a factory when the token can expire. a static string is applied as-is. the token is injected as . called once when a request returns 401. must return a new valid token. the failed request is retried exactly once with the new token. if refresh fails, fires and the error propagates to the caller. custom request signer — called after the bearer token is applied. use for hmac, api key rotation, or any custom signing scheme. static headers appended to every authenticated request. --- 401 vs 403 handling | response | behavior | | -------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | 401 | called once → request retried. if refresh fails → event + error propagates. | | 403 | error propagates immediately. is never called for 403. | do not lump 401 and 403 together in your error handling. a 403 is an access policy decision — retrying with a refreshed token will not help. check the server's entitlement configuration instead. auth events: --- retry policy the default retry policy retries failed network requests with exponential backoff. configure it by passing a partial map to — it is merged over , so only the codes you want to override need to appear: auth refresh retries are separate from the general retry policy — is called exactly once, not retried. --- inside plugins: plugins should use instead of the global . the parameter types the parsed response — no casts. the options' | | controls how the body is decoded; pass a custom to transform a body. the player's auth config and retry policy are applied automatically: if you need the raw object before it is dispatched for example, to add a signature, use in the auth config rather than building it manually in the plugin. --- updating auth at runtime replace auth config after setup — for example, when a long-lived token is refreshed by an external mechanism: this merges the provided partial config with the existing auth config. only the fields you provide are updated.

title: Plugin System Overview
description: What plugins are, the five-layer model, how kit plugins differ from library plugins and consumer plugins, and where to find each.
content: plugin system overview the player is split into plugins for everything that most players you find out there just come bundled with, whether you need them or not. the idea is that you can make your player as lean as you want, anywhere from just getting an audio tag to play so you can listen for events and control it, all the way up to the full setup of a streaming platform like nomercy tv. splitting it up this way also lets your bundler strip out all the unused code, so you ship the smallest build you can. it keeps a clean line between the generic stuff and your stuff too. the plugins that ship in the packages know how to do their job and nothing about your app, so they work for anyone. your own plugins are where the app-specific things live, like your server urls or auth, and they can reach for whatever they need. keeping those two apart is most of what keeps things sane as the app grows, and it really comes down to one thing: what a plugin is allowed to import is what decides where it belongs. the architecture page has the full picture, and plugins and adapters covers how a plugin differs from an adapter. layer placement the five-layer model determines where a plugin belongs: | layer | type | rule | | --- | --- | --- | | 4 | built-in plugin | ships in a package. generic behavior — no server urls, no app tokens. works for any consumer. | | 5 | consumer plugin | your app. can import from anywhere. contains nomercy server endpoints, signalr, auth tokens. | both layers use the same base class. the distinction is purely what they import and what goes in their options. --- plugin scopes plugins live at three different scopes: kit plugins shipped inside . these are generic audio, visualization, dom, and coordination plugins that work with any player built on the kit. most are in the main barrel export; a few use subpath exports. see built-in kit plugins for the full catalogue. library plugins shipped inside the video or music player packages. these are domain-specific to their media type, and each library documents its own. see the video player and music player sections for their plugin pages. consumer plugins written by you. named with a vendor prefix , . these live in your application codebase at layer 5. see plugin authoring for how to write one. --- registration and lookup for the full registration api see plugin registration. --- plugin contract every plugin must satisfy the conformance checklist in the plugin standard. the standard is enforced by lint rules in the kit. --- built-in kit plugin catalog these twelve plugins ship in . none are registered automatically. | plugin | what it does | import | | --- | --- | --- | | | creates and owns the + signal chain. required by all other audio plugins. | | | | mounts a shared and runs the raf render loop. required by visualization plugins. | | | | chromecast web sender sdk bridge — forwards player state to a cast receiver and mirrors it back. | | | | 10-band parametric eq with pre-gain, named presets, and persistence. requires . | | | | master gain + stereo pan with persistence. requires . | | | | fft analyser — emits events with frequency, waveform, and band-energy data. requires . | | | | abstract base class for canvas visualizations. subclass and override . requires + . | | | | bridge between a host page and a player running inside an . | | | | keyboard binding router. default bindings: space, arrow keys, . configurable scope and cooldown. | | | | wires — os lock-screen controls, hardware media keys, now playing artwork. | | | | toast notification overlay with transient, persistent, and queued modes. | | | | web locks–based cross-tab election so only one tab plays at a time. | | --- plugin or adapter? quick rule: adding something new the player does is a plugin; changing how it already does something is an adapter a port swap. they pair up nicely too, like a plugin that reads from a storage port you swapped. plugins and adapters walks through the boundary and when to reach for each. --- where to go next | goal | page | | --- | --- | | register, look up, or remove a plugin | plugin registration | | browse all kit-shipped plugins | built-in kit plugins | | write your own plugin | plugin authoring | | read the locked conformance standard | plugin standard | | browse adapter ports | adapter ports | | browse video-player plugins | video player section | | browse music-player plugins | music player section |

title: Adapters
description: The kit adapter ports. Name, purpose, default implementation, and how to replace each one.
content: kit adapter ports we provide the adapter pattern so you can change how the player behaves whenever you have a need that's a bit unique, something that shouldn't be the default for everyone. every piece here, like where state gets saved, how the player talks to a server, or which clock it reads, already has a sensible default wired in. you only reach for an adapter when that default doesn't fit you. say you want the player to remember resume positions and volume on your own server instead of in the browser, so they follow your users from their phone to their tv. you don't fork anything or go digging through player internals for that. you write a small storage adapter that reads and writes against your api, hand it to , and everything else carries on exactly as before. the player never knows where the bytes actually go, it just asks the port and gets an answer. that's really all a port is: a clearly defined slot with a default sitting in it. swapping what's in the slot is how you make the player yours without making it everyone's. this is also the line between an adapter and a plugin. if you're changing how something the player already does works on the inside, that's a port swap. if you're adding something new for the player to do, like an equalizer or a skip button, that's a plugin. plugins and adapters covers when to reach for each. the kit ships the content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-kit/src/adapters/clock/iclock.ts / iclock by default the player reads the wall-clock time through . that works fine in most situations. where it falls short is anything that needs to agree on the current moment across multiple devices: group listening sessions, watch parties, or any plugin that schedules actions against a server-side timeline. drifts per device, so two clients that think they're in sync can be off by hundreds of milliseconds. the clock port lets you supply a corrected time source without touching any plugin. you pass a plain function to , and anything that calls picks up your corrected value from that moment on. the interface is the shape you implement when you want a structured object, which you then hand over as . everything you import from this page lives in these two lines: built-in adapter a plain object that wraps . the kit uses this value whenever is not configured. you never construct it yourself, but you can import it to use as a fallback inside a custom clock or to verify the contract shape in tests. usage pass any zero-argument function returning a millisecond epoch timestamp: to use a structured implementation, bind its method: after setup, returns whatever your returns. plugins coordinating timestamps should call rather than directly so they transparently pick up any correction you install. interface one method. it returns the current time as a unix-epoch millisecond integer. the simplicity is intentional: anything that can produce a from a moment in time satisfies this contract. custom implementation the common case is a clock corrected by an ntp-style offset you fetch from your own backend: if the sync fails or hasn't run yet, stays 0 and the clock degrades gracefully to . this sync uses the platform on purpose, not the kit's built-in , because the round-trip measurement must not be thrown off by automatic retries. that is the exception, not the rule. for ordinary data requests, prefer the built-in client: outside a plugin, or inside one, so your auth and retry policy are applied for you. see auth and fetch. for tests, a controllable fake is the main use case: see also - adapters, the full port catalog - realtime, the websocket channel port, used by group-listening features that pair with a corrected clock

title: Element Factory
description: DOM element creation helpers, createElement, createButton, createSVG, addClasses, removeClasses, and their fluent builder types.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-kit/src/adapters/element-factory/dom.ts / element factory this is not an adapter port in the same sense as the logger or storage. there is no interface to swap and no option. it is a small set of dom utility functions that both player libraries and plugin authors use to create and configure elements without writing verbose chains. the fluent builder pattern means you can create, add classes, set attributes, and insert an element into the dom in one expression rather than four separate statements. all five functions are also available from the subpath: functions creates an element of with the given and returns a fluent builder. when is , an existing element with that is reused instead of creating a second one. this is useful for singleton overlays progress bar, subtitle container that a plugin might try to mount more than once. creates a with and both set to , and the click listener already attached. this is the baseline accessible button pattern the built-in ui plugins use for all controls. creates an element in the svg namespace with , , and set. returns the raw element so you can append , , or children directly. adds css class names to , skipping empty strings. returns a fluent builder so you can chain further operations. removes css class names from , skipping empty strings. returns directly not a builder since removal is typically the last step. builder types the fluent builders are typed so the chain narrows correctly as you go: call at the end of any chain to retrieve the underlying dom element. see also - adapters, the full port catalog

title: IEventBus
description: The event bus port, IEventBus interface, the built-in EventEmitter, and when you would ever swap it.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-kit/src/adapters/event-bus/ieventbus.ts / ieventbus the event bus is the connective tissue between the player, its plugins, and your application code. every , , , and call inside the kit goes through , the default implementation. you almost certainly never swap this out. it is wired internally before runs and is not a option. the only realistic reason to replace it is if you are embedding the player inside a reactive store system vuex, pinia, redux and want all events to flow through that store's own event mechanism instead. in that case you implement and hand it to the player constructor directly. built-in adapter a plain emitter. both player classes extend it, so calling is literally calling on the player instance. plugins access it through / , which delegate to the same player-scoped instance. a few design details worth knowing: - registering the same function reference twice for the same event adds it only once, the underlying deduplicates. - stores a wrapper in a keyed on the original handler reference, so can find and remove the wrapper even though the caller never touched it. - snapshots the listener set before iterating, so a handler calling mid-dispatch does not mutate the live iteration. - each listener is wrapped in a try/catch so one bad handler cannot abort the rest of the dispatch chain. - fires a microtask-delayed event when a previously empty event gains its first listener, useful for lazy-load logic. the phantom field on is a compile-time brand used by the generic type inference machinery. it is never assigned at runtime. interface removes every listener across all events. the player calls this during disposal to prevent handler leaks. returns the total live listener count across all events, which the testing leak harness uses to assert that plugins clean up after themselves across use-then-dispose cycles. when you'd replace it you probably won't. this port has no config key because the kit constructs the bus before runs. if you do need to replace it, the typical case is routing all player events through an existing pub/sub or store-event system so you can observe them in one place without adding a separate subscriber. implement with the store's publish/subscribe primitives, pass it to the player constructor, and the rest of the kit keeps calling without knowing anything changed. see also - adapters, the full port catalog - lifecycle registry, the other internal resource plugins depend on

title: IIdGenerator
description: The ID generator port, IIdGenerator interface, the built-in crypto.randomUUID adapter, and swapping it in tests.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-kit/src/adapters/id-generator/iidgenerator.ts / iidgenerator every plugin instance, every media item, and every internal resource the player creates needs a unique identifier. the kit calls to get one, and by default that means . this is almost entirely invisible to you during normal use. the one time you care is in tests: random uuids make snapshot assertions and deterministic test output painful. swapping in a sequential counter makes generated ids predictable and assertion-friendly. there is no key for this adapter. it is a construction-time concern, not a runtime configuration. built-in adapter a plain object that delegates to . in environments where is absent some older workers, non-secure contexts, it falls back to a + suffix, which is collision-resistant enough for non-cryptographic ids. the adapter is a plain object rather than a class because no state is needed: is a pure call with no side effects. interface that is the entire contract. one method, one return value, no configuration. when you'd replace it in production: never. the default is fine and you should not think about it. in tests: swap in a counter so your assertions are not fighting random uuids. the counter resets when you create a new generator instance, so each test suite starts from if you create a fresh one in . see also - adapters, the full port catalog

title: ILifecycleRegistry
description: The lifecycle registry port, ILifecycleRegistry interface, the built-in LifecycleRegistry, and what it tracks for automatic teardown.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-kit/src/adapters/lifecycle-registry/ilifecycleregistry.ts / ilifecycleregistry every plugin gets a lifecycle registry, and it is the main reason plugin authors almost never write manual cleanup code. any listener, timer, observer, fetch signal, or animation frame you register through the registry is automatically cancelled when the plugin is disposed. you never construct one yourself. the kit creates a fresh for each plugin instance and hands it to the plugin as . you call its methods to register resources, and handles the rest in a single call when the player or plugin tears down. there is no key for this adapter. it is an internal construction detail, not a configurable option. built-in adapter tracks six categories of disposable resource: dom event listeners, timers, intervals, disconnect-able observers , , etc., instances, and loops. tears them all down in order: listeners first, then timers and intervals, then raf loops, then observers, then abort controllers, and finally user-registered cleanup callbacks in reverse registration order most-recently-registered runs first, like a stack unwind. is idempotent: calling it twice is safe, the second call is a no-op. if is called after , the callback runs immediately rather than being queued. interface a few things worth noting: - returns the observer unchanged so you can chain: . - is a no-op in ssr environments where is absent. - and return after disposal rather than a live timer id. - exceptions thrown inside timeout, interval, frame, and cleanup callbacks are caught and logged so one bad callback does not abort the teardown sequence. when you'd replace it almost never. the built-in implementation covers everything plugin authors need and its behaviour is well-defined. the one hypothetical: if you are running the player in a custom environment where the web apis , , are shimmed or unavailable, you might need a registry that delegates to those shims. in that case, implement with your environment's equivalents. see also - adapters, the full port catalog - event bus, the other core internal both players and plugins share

title: ILogger
description: The logging port, ILogger interface, the built-in Logger, adding a sink, and wiring a custom logger like Pino or Sentry.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-kit/src/adapters/logger/ilogger.ts / ilogger by default the player and all its plugins log through a small console logger. how noisy it gets is gated by the you set at , which is fine while you're building. in production you usually want those lines going somewhere you can actually see them, like sentry breadcrumbs or your own telemetry. you also don't want every plugin to know about it. the logger port is how you do that from one place. most of the time you don't even replace it: you add a sink to the built-in logger and let your console logs flow to a second destination too. when you'd rather route everything through a logging library you already use, you wrap that library in the shape and hand it to . either way, the kit and every plugin keep calling and never notice the difference. everything you import from this page lives in these two lines: built-in adapter a console logger that supports multiple sinks. the kit creates one root instance per player, and every plugin shares it through a scoped . you only construct one yourself when you want to pre-register a sink before handing it to . log levels levels run from quiet to loud: , , , , , . each line emits only when the active threshold is at or above its level. the default is , and you set it with at setup rather than touching the logger directly: adding a sink this is the common case, and it doesn't replace anything. build the default , attach a sink, and pass it in. your normal console output keeps working; the sink just gets a copy. interface plugin authors never construct a logger. they receive already scoped to their plugin id, so anything they log shows up tagged with where it came from. custom implementation when you'd rather route everything through a logging library you already run, wrap it in : if your logging library has no multi-sink concept, keeping one destination and no-opping is fine. just document it, like the comment above does. see also - metrics and diagnostics, what the player logs and measures - adapters, the full port catalog

title: IMediaList
description: The media list port, IMediaList interface, the built-in MediaList, cursor semantics, and the full mutation and event API.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-kit/src/adapters/media-list/imedialist.ts / imedialist both and use a single instance as their queue. rather than maintaining parallel list state in each library, all queue methods delegate here: append, remove, shuffle, sort, and everything else. the list is cursor-aware, meaning it always knows which item is current and keeps the cursor stable as items are added, removed, or reordered around it. you almost never replace this. there is no key for it. replacing it would only make sense if you needed the queue to be backed by an external data source a server-side playlist api, an indexeddb store rather than kept in memory. built-in adapter an in-memory, cursor-aware list that extends . must extend , which requires at minimum an field. cursor semantics: - is when items exist and when the list is empty. - every mutation that shifts item positions also shifts the cursor to keep it pointing at the same item. removing the item before the current decrements the cursor by one. removing the current item clamps the cursor to the new last index. - accepts the item itself, its , a zero-based index, or a predicate function, first match wins. every mutation method fires a specific event followed by a event. subscribe to when you only care that something changed. subscribe to the narrower events , , , etc. when you need to know what changed. interface events emits these events. fires after every other mutation event. | event | payload | |-------|---------| | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | a few method notes: - preserves the cursor by item when possible. if the previously current item is still in the new list, the cursor moves to its new index. if not, the cursor resets to . - replaces an item by in place, no cursor change, no events. callers that need to notify listeners must do so themselves. - does nothing if or either index is out of range. - uses fisher-yates and the cursor follows the current item to its new position. - also follows the current item after reordering. - clears all items, resets the cursor to , and removes all event listeners. when you'd replace it the in-memory default is sufficient for most players. if you need the queue to reflect a server-side playlist that can be updated externally e.g. a shared watch party queue, you would implement backed by that remote state and emit the same events when it changes. notice this calls rather than the platform . is the kit's built-in client, so your bearer token, retry policy, and events all come along for free. inside a plugin you reach the exact same client through . reach for the built-in one by default and only drop to the platform when you have a reason to. see auth and fetch. see also - title: IUrlResolver
description: The URL resolver port, IUrlResolver interface, ResolvedUrl, UrlCategory, and wiring a custom CDN signing or per-category routing resolver.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-kit/src/adapters/url-resolver/iurlresolver.ts / iurlresolver every url the player touches, whether a media manifest, a subtitle file, a poster image, or a drm license endpoint, passes through the url resolver before it reaches a element, a worker, or a cast receiver. the built-in resolver applies your token-injection callback and then parses the result into a structured you can inspect. that covers most cases. where you need more is when different asset types need different treatment. a cdn might require per-request signed urls on media and subtitles, but let poster images through unsigned. a multi-origin setup might route files to one edge and font assets to another. the port handles all of that from one place, and the rest of the kit never knows the difference. you supply a resolver at or swap it at runtime with . when you only need to extend the built-in behavior rather than replace it, call inside your resolver and let the default path handle any category you don't want to intercept. everything you import from this page lives in these two lines: built-in adapter there is no exported class for the default resolver. when no is configured, the player applies to the raw url string and parses the result into a internally. if you only need to add an auth token to every request, is the right place for it and you do not need to supply a at all. url categories the kit passes a category string alongside every url so your resolver can branch on asset type. the built-in category constants are: custom plugins may pass any string. your resolver should treat unknown categories as a passthrough rather than an error. the resolvedurl shape your resolver returns a object. the player hands this directly to the appropriate consumer, so is what ends up in or the cast receiver. use to gate on file type. it strips query strings for you, so gives , not . the urlresolvercontext shape the second argument to your resolver function carries everything you need to make a routing decision: call to delegate back to the built-in pipeline for any category you don't want to handle yourself. interface a resolver is a callable interface, not a class. the simplest valid implementation is a plain function. custom implementation the common case is signing media and subtitle urls with a short-lived cdn token while leaving everything else to the default pipeline: the token fetch uses , the kit's built-in client, so it carries your auth and retry policy automatically. inside a plugin the same client is , and you should prefer it over the platform by default. see auth and fetch. you can also swap the resolver after setup, for example when the user switches between a public and authenticated session: for multi-origin routing, where different asset types come from different hosts: see also - logger, the logging port - adapters, the full port catalog

title: ABR and Bandwidth
description: bandwidth(), bandwidthEstimator(), canPlay(), and CanPlayResult — throughput estimation and device capability probing.
content: abr and bandwidth three methods that expose throughput estimation and decode-capability probing. bandwidthestimator read or replace the bandwidth estimator function. reading returns the currently wired estimator or if none is set. writing installs a custom estimator. the active stream source calls the function on every abr level decision. install your own estimator when you have out-of-band signal signalr quality report, server-sent bitrate hint that is more accurate than the default download-speed measurement. the estimator is called synchronously on the abr decision path — keep it fast. --- canplay probes whether the browser can decode a specific media profile smoothly. delegates to the platform adapter's bridge, which wraps the standard api. --- canplayresult means the codec is not supported — do not select this quality level. means the level is playable but the browser may drop frames under load — use as a last resort only. is typically seen on mobile devices with high-bitrate streams that the cpu decodes in software rather than through the hardware decoder pipeline. it is informational — takes precedence for quality selection. --- using canplay for quality filtering before rendering a quality picker, filter out levels the browser cannot handle: for hls streams, the video player's hdr-aware abr logic does this filtering automatically — it uses internally to exclude hdr levels on sdr displays. calling manually is only needed when building a custom quality ui that must pre-filter the level list. --- see also - media tracks — and - player state — for the abr/manual mode flag - metrics — in - platform — the platform port

title: Plugin Authoring
description: How to write a plugin for the NoMercy Player SDK. Lifecycle, events, error handling, advisories, and the conformance checklist.
content: plugin authoring plugins are the extension point for the player sdk. every feature beyond core transport lives in a plugin — the built-in ui, eq, lyrics, skip markers, chromecast handoff. your app-specific features follow the same contract. for the locked conformance document that lint rules enforce, see plugin standard. minimal plugin skeleton usage: --- identity fields every plugin must declare three static fields: the is the globally unique key. kit-shipped plugins use bare kebab-case , . third-party plugins must use a vendor prefix , . --- lifecycle is called during . return a if you need to load config or register async resources — fires only after all plugins' promises resolve. is called on or . all timers, intervals, animation frames, and dom mounts registered through the plugin's helper methods , , , auto-dispose — you only need to explicitly clean up external resources. --- event listening always use inside a plugin, never . the form auto-disposes with the plugin. , , and have the same overloaded shapes. --- emitting events --- error handling never throw raw errors or call directly. use aborts the current flow, returns or surfaces without aborting. both carry a that decides what the error means: | severity | channel | aborts flow? | meaning | | -------- | ------- | ------------ | ------- | | | | yes | unrecoverable — the player is going down. consumer tears down or shows a fatal screen. | | | + | yes | recoverable — this operation failed, but the plugin keeps running for future events. | | | + | no | degradation — playback continues, consumer is informed. | | | | no | observability only. | does not auto-dispose the player — it raises the contract-level "shutting down" signal. the consumer decides the teardown: disabling a plugin in response to an error is a separate concern — declare it as a recovery action, not a severity. --- static error recovery declare a recovery policy to control what happens when a specific error code is emitted by the player or by a dependency: options: | | | . the player's can override these per-consumer. --- plugin dependencies declare required or optional plugin dependencies using class references — never string ids: --- phase advisories declare which phases are safe for each method. the kit surfaces these as warnings in development: --- plugin replacement and extension replace a built-in plugin with the same id: extend without replacing: --- dom and storage --- testing provides a fresh player with the plugin registered and auto-disposes in . --- conformance checklist before shipping a plugin: - is vendored - is a valid semver string - is a one-liner - and are defined or inherited - all listeners use never - all timers use / / - all errors use / - every mutator has a paired reader - plugin's generic is declared and exported - is declared when depending on other plugins - tests cover behavior and

title: Persistence
description: Choosing a storage backend, saving playback position, and restoring it on the next page load.
content: persistence read this when you need to save and restore playback state across page loads — resume position, last-played track, volume level, subtitle preferences. the kit's storage adapter system handles all of this. prerequisites: kit — adapters covers the three built-in storage backends. what the player persists automatically with the default , the player saves and restores: - volume level - mute state - subtitle language preference the last selected language - audio language preference - eq state if is registered - subtitle style preferences if is registered playback position is not saved automatically — that requires a consumer plugin because the player does not know where your server stores watch history. --- saving and restoring playback position write a consumer plugin that saves position to your backend: register it: --- local-only position saving no server for a purely client-side implementation, use directly: reads from the same backend the player is configured with. keys are automatically namespaced. --- choosing the right storage backend for your context | scenario | backend | | ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | standard web app | default | | ssr next.js, nuxt | on server, on client — see advanced: ssr | | test suite | — no cross-test contamination | | large eq preset library | | | sync across devices | custom backend calling your api | --- indexeddb backend for large data eq snapshots, subtitle caches: is async internally but the interface is synchronous. writes are fire-and-forget; reads return the last committed value. for a fully async custom backend, see advanced: custom adapter. --- what to read next - kit — adapters — full interface and the backend catalog - advanced: custom adapter — writing an async indexeddb-worker backend - recipes: lyrics and equalizer — eq state is persisted through this same storage system

title: Auth and Tokens
description: Wiring the authFetch wrapper, handling refresh-on-401, ensuring 403 propagates, and writing a custom auth adapter.
content: auth and tokens read this when your media sources require authorization — hls streams behind a cdn auth wall, apis that return 401 when tokens expire, or endpoints that enforce access control via 403. prerequisites: the auth config is the same on video and music players. for the full reference see kit — auth & fetch. 401 vs 403 — a hard rule | status | what happens | | ------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | 401 | called once → request retried with new token → if refresh fails, fires | | 403 | error propagates immediately. is never called. | do not lump 401 and 403 in the same catch block. a 403 is an entitlement decision — retrying with a refreshed token achieves nothing. the right response to a 403 is to check the user's subscription or permissions on your server. --- static vs factory token use the factory form whenever the token can expire. a stale static string will cause 401s until the page is refreshed. --- updating auth at runtime after , replace the auth config without recreating the player: useful when a user signs in during a session or when a long-lived token is refreshed by an external mechanism. --- static extra headers add headers to every authenticated request e.g. app version, device id: --- custom request signing hmac, signed urls for non-bearer auth schemes, use : is called after is applied. both can be used together. --- using authfetch inside plugins inside a plugin, always use instead of the global . this applies the player's auth config, respects the retry policy, and integrates with error reporting: --- retry policy the default retry policy retries failed network requests 3 times with exponential backoff. auth refresh retries are separate — is called exactly once, never retried. to tune the general retry behavior, pass a partial map to . it is merged over : --- what to read next - kit — auth & fetch — full interface reference - advanced: custom adapter — writing a fully custom auth adapter for non-standard signing schemes - recipes: persistence — auth tokens + watch position working together

title: Troubleshooting
description: Common setup and runtime problems with the NoMercy Player SDK. Symptoms, causes, and fixes — verified against kit source.
content: troubleshooting every entry below is verified against the kit source. if the symptom you're hitting isn't here, file an issue with a minimal reproduction. player never reaches symptom: hangs indefinitely. the event never fires. causes and fixes: 1. a plugin's returned a promise that never resolves. awaits all promises capped by , default 10 seconds before emitting . audit each registered plugin for async work without timeouts. 2. the container element doesn't exist in the dom at . the kit doesn't wait for the element to appear. ensure returns a non-null element before calling . 3. a plugin's rejected. check the console for events. the failed plugin is disabled; still fires for the remaining plugins. if you see no and no , the promise is stuck see 1. 4. you're inspecting the wrong instance. returns the same instance on every call with the same id. if two parts of your code call setup on different ids, they're different players. --- dev mode — hls manifest fails to load symptom: locally served files fail when opening the html directly via . cause: browser security policy blocks cross-origin requests from origins. hls segment fetches from any other origin including are blocked. fix: serve over : or use vite / webpack dev server / any local http server. --- framework ssr — player crashes during server-side render symptom: build or render crashes with or during ssr next.js, nuxt, sveltekit, astro. cause: the player depends on browser apis , , , . these don't exist in a node server environment. fix: lazy-load the player on the client only. next.js react: nuxt / vue: astro: use so the component never renders on the server. pick the directive that matches the component's framework: sveltekit: guard with from , or use which only fires client-side. --- two players on the same page share state symptom: two players appear to share state — controlling one affects the other. cause: and are factories backed by an internal registry. calls with the same return the same instance. two components using the same id are pointing at the same player. fix: use unique ids per instance: for a single-player app, picking a static id is fine. for multi-player uis pip, watch parties, tile grids, generate a stable id per slot. --- volume resets every page load symptom: the player ignores the user's saved volume preference. cause: the kit doesn't auto-persist volume — that's a plugin concern. fix: persist it in a small plugin via the namespaced storage adapter , not raw . volume is on the 0–100 scale. --- thrown by music player method symptom: calling on a music player throws with code . cause: audio backends don't have subtitle tracks. is on the shared player surface but is intentionally not implemented on . fix: catch the error by type. import from the kit: or — simpler — only call on video players. --- , , or throws on symptom: adding these music-player plugins, then fires with a . still fires for the remaining plugins. cause: all three are stubbed in and intentionally throw . full implementations are planned for . fix: don't register them yet. track progress in versioning. --- hls auth — segments return 401 after a delay symptom: hls manifest loads, playback starts, then segment requests start returning 401 after some time. or every segment 401s from the first request. cause token expiry: is a static string. the kit injects whatever value you passed at setup. if the token expires between manifest load and segment fetch, the injected value is stale. cause no refresh: isn't configured. the kit retries a 401 exactly once if a refresh function is provided; without it, the request fails immediately. fix: pass as a factory and provide a refresh function: the factory is called on every authenticated request — the player always sees the current token. on a 401, is called once and the request retries automatically. a 403 propagates and is never retried — that's an access-policy problem on the server, not an auth-token problem. --- inline of the kit fails — symptom: a consumer or a custom plugin imports from and the resolver can't find it. cause: the kit is the foundation under both and but isn't a transitive runtime dependency a consumer would see. if you're writing a plugin or adapter against the kit directly, you need to install the kit alongside. fix: if you only use the video or music package's surface no custom plugins, you don't need this — the per-library package re-exports what you need. --- container element class never updates symptom: the container should gain / etc. but the classes are missing. cause: state classes live on the element passed as to . if you re-mount the player into a fresh dom node e.g. ssr hydration replacing the host element, the kit's reference is to the old node. fix: don't re-create the container after setup. if you have to hmr, spa navigation, the player first and again on the new node. state classes are owned by the kit itself, not by — you get them even on a raw html container with no ui plugin installed. --- custom plugin's never fires symptom: a plugin declares with recovery actions but nothing happens when it throws. cause: is a declarative map — . the kit consults it when the plugin throws via . if your plugin throws directly with or emits via , the recovery map is bypassed. fix: always raise plugin errors through the base class helper: see plugin standard §1.8 for the full error escalation contract. --- plugin runs twice / plugin event listeners double up symptom: event handlers in a plugin's fire twice for every event. cause: most commonly, is being called manually in addition to the player calling it. don't invoke yourself — triggers the lifecycle. second cause: two different classes share the same . the kit allows this for replacement subclass with same id replaces the original but if both are added independently, both register and both listen. fix: ensure each plugin id is unique. use ids for third-party plugins , to avoid collisions with kit-shipped plugins. --- reporting a bug if the symptom isn't here, file an issue with: - kit version from - player package + version - browser + version - minimal html/js reproduction a public codesandbox / stackblitz link is ideal - console output with enabled

title: Multi-Instance
description: Running multiple players on one page — PiP + main player, watch-party tile grid, tab-leader pattern, and event-bus isolation between instances.
content: multi-instance read this when you need more than one player active on the same page — a mini-player or pip alongside a main player, a grid of synchronized tiles, or a podcast player running in the background while a video plays. two players on one page --- pip + main player pattern the browser's native picture-in-picture api keeps one element in a floating window. the player exposes pip control: no second player instance is needed for native pip — the single player's element moves to the pip window. --- watch-party tile grid for a grid of synchronized tiles each playing the same content: --- tab-leader pattern when multiple browser tabs have the same player open e.g. a podcast player that persists across navigation, elect a leader tab that owns playback. other tabs follow. use for cross-tab communication: in practice, use the watchpartyliteplugin worked example as a starting point and extend it with a leader election algorithm. --- event-bus isolation two player instances never share an event bus. if you need a player to react to another player's events, wire them explicitly: for more complex cross-instance protocols, write a coordinator object outside both players: --- storage namespace isolation each player's storage is namespaced by its . two players with ids and write to different storage keys: - - if you want two players to share a storage state e.g. the same volume preference, pass the same backend instance through and use a shared key namespace: --- what to read next - advanced: custom plugin — the watch-party-lite plugin for cross-instance sync - advanced: embedding — cross-frame iframe player control - advanced: performance — memory budget when running multiple instances
